stories.headline: IMD warns of possible cyclone formation in Bay of Bengal by Monday
stories.title: IMD warns of possible cyclone formation in Bay of Bengal by Monday
stories.summary: IMD warns of possible cyclone formation in Bay of Bengal by Monday
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: A weather system developing over the southeast Bay of Bengal is likely to intensify into a cyclonic storm by Monday evening and could further strengthen into a severe cyclonic storm, the India Meteorological Department (IMD) has forecast.
Amid the possibility of worsening weather conditions, fishermen have been advised to return to shore, with strong winds expected over the southwest Bay of Bengal until 18 November.
The Indian Coast Guard has also stepped up its preparedness, keeping ships and aircraft on standby to carry out rescue operations and safeguard lives and property.
According to the IMD, the low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify on Sunday while moving west-northwestwards.
It is likely to develop into a cyclonic storm over the central parts of the southeast Bay of Bengal by Monday evening.
The weather system could gain further strength after reaching cyclonic storm intensity, with the possibility of developing into a severe cyclonic storm.
However, the IMD has not yet specified any likely landfall location or timing.
The extent of the potential impact along the coast also remains unclear.
The immediate weather advisories include warnings of strong winds over the southwest Bay of Bengal and rainfall across parts of Tamil Nadu.
The IMD has forecast moderate rainfall on Sunday and Monday in districts adjoining the Western Ghats and southern parts of Tamil Nadu.
Chennai may also experience light rainfall on Sunday, according to the regional weather centre.
The strong wind warning over the southwest Bay of Bengal remains in effect until Wednesday, 18 November.

stories.headline: The oldest trap in the spy’s book
stories.title: The oldest trap in the spy’s book
stories.summary: Wars today are fought with drones, malware, and artificial intelligence. Yet two recent news reports show that the spy’s most dependable weapon is still the oldest one: a flattering stranger and a man who wants to be admired. In New Delhi, a police chargesheet accuses a serving Indian Air Force Wing Commander, arrested under the Official Secrets Act, of passing classified details to a suspected Pakistani intelligence operative. The leaked material allegedly included secret war plans, the strength of a covert drone unit, and fighter deployments in Leh. Police say the two chatted on WhatsApp for months until the officer was caught carrying a smartphone inside his office. Shockingly, he allegedly traded pages of a secret war plan in exchange for explicit photographs, and even installed spyware on the phones of five subordinates. Around the same time in the United States, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports of an affair with Alice Huang, a woman of no relation whom American officials suspect was passing information to the Chinese government. While Beijing has dismissed the claims and it remains unclear what, if anything, was leaked, intelligence experts point out that a secret relationship at that level is a major security risk on its own. Honey trapping is one of the oldest tricks in espionage. Sometimes targets are blackmailed after being lured into compromising situations; other times, an intelligence agency notices a natural relationship developing and pressures the partner to spy. History shows that even trained professionals are not immune. In the 1960s, for instance, French diplomat Bernard Boursicot fell into a secret romance with a Peking opera singer in China. Chinese intelligence agents eventually told him he could only keep seeing his partner if he handed over embassy documents, and he complied for years. In today’s digital age, this threat has spread far beyond high-profile officials and corporate leaders. With social media and encrypted messaging apps, cybercriminals now run honey traps on an industrial scale, targeting ordinary citizens. Fake profiles, flattering messages, and staged video calls are routinely used to lure unsuspecting people into compromising positions, leaving common victims trapped in endless cycles of financial extortion and public humiliation. Such traps succeed because they exploit basic human psychology. The German philosopher Friedrich Nietzsche never wrote about espionage, yet he understood how easily people are drawn into dangerous situations when they lower their guard. As he famously warned, “When you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes back.” A honey trap is simply that abyss dressed up as affection. Victims are rarely fools; they are often capable men who trust their own judgment too much. Men in top positions are usually surrounded by obedience, not genuine admiration, so a stranger who makes them feel truly appreciated can quickly become a blind spot. These incidents prove a vital lesson: beyond high intelligence and sharp professional skills, moral integrity is equally important for anyone holding a high post. Rank and cleverness offer no protection when personal discipline fails. For those in positions of authority, caution is the best defence. Unexplained attention and sudden flattery from strangers must always be viewed with suspicion. Official work should never enter private chats, as a document sent over WhatsApp is beyond your control the moment you press send, and intimate photographs must never be exchanged since they become permanent tools for blackmail. Above all, remember that any relationship you have to hide from your organisation is already a serious liability. Shame only works in secret, so reporting a suspicious approach early allows your institution to manage the risk before it turns into a disaster. The write is a Kashmir based academic and teaches Political Science in the Higher Education Department of J&K.

stories.headline: Trump's Board of Peace faces its biggest test over Gaza
stories.title: Trump's Board of Peace faces its biggest test over Gaza
stories.summary: The Board of Peace, set up under US President Donald Trump's initiative, is approaching a crucial stage. Seen as an important effort to end the Gaza conflict and bring lasting peace to the Palestinian, the question now is: can it deliver on the ground? Its objectives included ending hostilities, moving Gaza away from Hamas rule, ensuring the withdrawal of Israeli forces and beginning reconstruction. A year back, the Board was formally launched with Trump as its chairman. The initiative received a lot of international backing through UN Security Council Resolution 2803. Its February 19 meeting in Washington further raised expectations, with several countries announcing financial commitments for Gaza's reconstruction. There has been some progress. The October 2025 ceasefire, the return of all hostages, the release of Palestinian prisoners and the expansion of humanitarian assistance were important developments. The Board's May 2026 report to the Security Council also referred to the establishment of an international organisation, a 28-member National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), preparations for an International Stabilisation Force (ISF) and reconstruction pledges amounting to $17 billion. Five countries: Albania, Indonesia, Kazakhstan, Kosovo and Morocco expressed their intention to contribute troops to the proposed stabilisation force. A pre-deployment assessment was also completed in April. These developments suggest that the Board has moved forward positively and has started putting an institutional structure in place. However, the Board's next phase of the peace plan looks somewhat stranded. Hamas and other Palestinian groups are expected to surrender civilian governance and security responsibilities to the NCAG. The proposed international force would monitor the ceasefire, support humanitarian deliveries and help train Palestinian police. Israel, meanwhile, is expected to withdraw in stages, while the process of disarming armed groups would be monitored. Reconstruction is also expected to begin under the supervision of the Board and the Palestinian technocratic administration. Israel and Hamas, the two major players in the conflict were supposed to cooperate but it is not happening. Scattered violence in Gaza continues. Civilians’ deaths continue. Hospitals remain under threat and displaced families cannot return to their homes. The recent Israeli strike on Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis on November 11, which killed at least six people, including a doctor and a 13-year-old boy, once again exposed the fragile situation. The Israeli military said it had targeted a Hamas commander and militants allegedly operating from the hospital. Hamas denied using the hospital complex for military purposes. The Board deplored the civilian casualties and called on Israel and Hamas to honour their commitments under the peace plan. It also urged all parties to protect civilians and provide the necessary authority and operational space for establishing secure, demilitarised medical facilities. Earlier, the Board had criticised Israel's response to flooding in Gaza and called for the entry of shelter, sanitation, drainage and winter supplies. Political observers feel that issuing statements is not enough. The real question is whether the Board can prevent further violence and ensure that humanitarian assistance reaches those who need it. According to the UN's November 5 humanitarian situation report, 1,593 Palestinians had been reported killed and 5,748 injured since the ceasefire agreement. Nearly two million Palestinians remain displaced, with homes, hospitals and essential infrastructure destroyed. For ordinary Palestinians, the success of the Board will be judged by whether they can live without fear, get medical treatment, receive food and shelter and return to a normal life. If these basic conditions cannot be ensured, the Board's claims of progress will always be questioned. Political commentators observe that the main problem is not administrative but political. Israel insists that Hamas must be disarmed before reconstruction can proceed. Hamas, on the other hand, is reluctant to surrender its weapons and political influence without clear guarantees about Palestinian rights, Israeli withdrawal and the future governance of Gaza. There is a roadmap. But who will ensure that both sides honour their commitments? The proposed International Stabilisation Force is central to the entire arrangement. Its success will depend on how many countries contribute troops, what powers the force is given, and whether it can operate effectively without being drawn into another confrontation. Civilians living there must feel that they are regaining control over their lives and institutions. There are also questions about the Board's own structure. It raises concerns about accountability and continuity. The Board has the endorsement of the UN Security Council for its role in Gaza, but it is not a replacement for the United Nations. It does not have the same universal authority or enforcement powers as the Security Council. Its strength depends on political influence, financial support and the willingness of participating countries to cooperate. The Board's credibility will depend on how it is viewed by Palestinians, Israel and the wider international community. For Palestinians, the immediate priorities are security, food, shelter, functioning hospitals and schools. For Israel, the priority is a guarantee that Hamas will not rebuild its military capabilities. For the international community, the question is whether the Board can function as an impartial peace mechanism or will remain largely an extension of American foreign policy. Some European countries have also expressed reservations about its mandate and its relationship with existing UN institutions. France and other critics have stressed that its activities should remain focused on Gaza. The Board will also have to ensure transparency in the use of reconstruction funds. Financial pledges running into billions of dollars will mean little unless the money reaches Gaza and produces visible improvements in people's lives. The Board no doubt has provided a diplomatic framework, secured financial commitments and established administrative arrangements. But it would be premature to describe it as a successful peace mechanism. It has made progress in setting up the structure, but its ability to enforce decisions remains still at a distance. Last week's US midterm election results have introduced an important political factor. The Democrats have secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate. This may be a major setback for Trump, who began his second term with Republicans controlling both chambers. The new Congress will take office on January 3, 2027. But the election outcome has already changed the political atmosphere in Washington. For the Board of Peace, this could have consequences. A Democratic-controlled Congress is likely to scrutinise the administration's financial commitments, reconstruction spending and wider West Asia policy more closely. It may seek answers about the Board's functioning. This may put additional pressure on Trump to demonstrate that his peace initiative is delivering results. However, the election results do not mean the Board will automatically cease to function. Foreign policy and diplomatic negotiations remain largely within the authority of the President and the executive branch. Trump will continue as chairman of the Board, and the new Congress cannot simply remove him from that position. However, congressional control matters. Funding, oversight and political pressure can influence the extent of American support for the initiative. Domestic political battles could divert his attention and reduce the personal involvement that has so far driven the Board. The real test will be whether he treats the initiative as a lasting international commitment or primarily as an achievement associated with his presidency. The coming months are crucial and will determine whether the Board can turn its plans into reality. Without accountability, the ceasefire will remain vulnerable to repeated breakdowns. For India, developments in Gaza are important for several reasons. Stability in West Asia is closely linked to India's energy security, trade and the safety of millions of Indians living and working in the region. New Delhi has consistently supported a negotiated two-state solution and would want Gaza's reconstruction to take place through a credible process. Ultimately, the Board faces three difficult questions. Can it persuade Israel to exercise restraint and withdraw in accordance with an agreed framework? Can it ensure that Hamas gives up its armed and governing role? And can it provide Palestinians with a functioning administration and a genuine political future? The Board is yet to prove that it can guarantee peace. It has moved beyond announcements and created an institutional framework. However, continuing violence, the humanitarian crisis and uncertainty over the international force show how far it remains from achieving its objectives. The Board still has an opportunity to prove that it can make a difference. But its credibility will not be decided in Washington or at international conferences. It will be judged at ground zero, in Gaza's hospitals, on its damaged streets and among the families waiting to return to their homes. Authour is National Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: India should become developer, innovator and global leader in advanced tech: Rajnath
stories.title: India should become developer, innovator and global leader in advanced tech: Rajnath
stories.summary: New Delhi, Nov 15: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh on Sunday called for making India not merely a user of advanced technologies, but also a developer, innovator and global leader in critical domains, as he emphasised the need to strengthen the country’s non-destructive testing ecosystem for better preparedness and self-reliance. He virtually addressed the 36th Annual Conference on Non-Destructive Evaluation & Enabling Technologies and the 15th International Symposium on Non-Destructive Testing in Aerospace. Singh stressed the importance of developing indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, promoting consistent quality assurance practices and ensuring the accuracy, reliability and integrity of testing results, particularly in strategic applications. He asserted that there can be no compromise on the integrity of testing results in strategic applications. "We must strengthen our indigenous capabilities in advanced inspection technologies, specialised sensors, evaluation equipment and associated software," the minister asserted. "Developing domestic capabilities in these areas is essential for reducing technological dependencies and securing critical defence supply chains. We must promote consistent quality assurance practices across the entire defence industrial ecosystem," he said. Public sector undertakings, private manufacturers, start-ups and MSMEs have an "important role to play" in this endeavour. "We must ensure that inspection results are accurate, reliable and traceable, and are based on robust procedures and appropriate standards followed by assessment by qualified professionals,” the defence minister said. The three-day conference, organised by the Indian Society for Non-Destructive Testing in Hyderabad, Telangana, has brought together over 2,000 professionals, researchers, industry experts and students to deliberate on the latest advancements, emerging technologies and applications in non-destructive testing (NDT), the defence ministry said. Singh stressed that the NDT technologies enable examination of the integrity of materials, components and structures without causing any damage to them. Elucidating the concept, he said that just as ultrasound and X-rays help examine the human body without surgical intervention, NDT techniques enable the detection of internal defects in critical components without dismantling or damaging them. Singh underlined that as Indian defence systems become increasingly sophisticated, every critical material, component, assembly and manufacturing process must meet the highest standards of quality and reliability. “Hidden defects can affect operational availability, increase maintenance requirements, reduce the service life of equipment and, in critical situations, jeopardise mission success. We need to move beyond a culture of merely identifying defects towards actively preventing them by embedding quality at every stage of the manufacturing process,” he said. Singh stressed that the progress of a nation depends not merely on the technologies it develops, but also on the quality, reliability and security of the systems it builds. In defence applications, including missiles, aircraft, naval platforms and spacecraft, quality is not merely a manufacturing requirement but an essential element of operational reliability and national security, he said. Emphasising the strategic significance of the sector, Singh said that for a country aspiring to achieve technological leadership, the importance of NDT cannot be overstated. He asserted that India's pursuit of “Aatmanirbharta (self-reliance)” in defence is not merely an economic objective but also a strategic necessity. Underscoring the importance of keeping pace with the rapidly changing global security environment, Singh said indigenous weapons, platforms and supporting systems "must deliver the highest levels of reliability and performance at all times". He urged professionals associated with the NDT sector to continuously upgrade their capabilities and keep the spirit of innovation alive in sync with emerging technologies and evolving security requirements. On the technological transformation underway in the field of non-destructive evaluation, he stressed that artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, advanced sensors, digital twins and predictive analytics are significantly expanding the possibilities of inspection and structural health monitoring. These technologies, he said, can improve the speed and consistency of inspections, facilitate the analysis of complex data and identify patterns that may not be easily detectable through conventional methods. Singh emphasised that the future lies in the intelligent integration of established inspection techniques with advanced digital technologies to make inspection processes more accurate, efficient and responsive to emerging industrial requirements. The minister called upon India to move beyond merely adopting these technologies and develop indigenous solutions tailored to its strategic and industrial requirements. Investment in research, advanced equipment, software and skilled manpower would strengthen domestic capabilities and enable Indian technologies to find markets internationally, he said.

Singh underlined that as Indian defence systems become increasingly sophisticated, every critical material, component, assembly and manufacturing process must meet the highest standards of quality and reliability.
“Hidden defects can affect operational availability, increase maintenance requirements, reduce the service life of equipment and, in critical situations, jeopardise mission success.
We need to move beyond a culture of merely identifying defects towards actively preventing them by embedding quality at every stage of the manufacturing process,” he said.
Singh stressed that the progress of a nation depends not merely on the technologies it develops, but also on the quality, reliability and security of the systems it builds.

In defence applications, including missiles, aircraft, naval platforms and spacecraft, quality is not merely a manufacturing requirement but an essential element of operational reliability and national security, he said.
Emphasising the strategic significance of the sector, Singh said that for a country aspiring to achieve technological leadership, the importance of NDT cannot be overstated.
He asserted that India's pursuit of “Aatmanirbharta (self-reliance)” in defence is not merely an economic objective but also a strategic necessity.

Underscoring the importance of keeping pace with the rapidly changing global security environment, Singh said indigenous weapons, platforms and supporting systems "must deliver the highest levels of reliability and performance at all times".

He urged professionals associated with the NDT sector to continuously upgrade their capabilities and keep the spirit of innovation alive in sync with emerging technologies and evolving security requirements.

On the technological transformation underway in the field of non-destructive evaluation, he stressed that artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, advanced sensors, digital twins and predictive analytics are significantly expanding the possibilities of inspection and structural health monitoring.

These technologies, he said, can improve the speed and consistency of inspections, facilitate the analysis of complex data and identify patterns that may not be easily detectable through conventional methods.

Singh emphasised that the future lies in the intelligent integration of established inspection techniques with advanced digital technologies to make inspection processes more accurate, efficient and responsive to emerging industrial requirements.
The minister called upon India to move beyond merely adopting these technologies and develop indigenous solutions tailored to its strategic and industrial requirements.
Investment in research, advanced equipment, software and skilled manpower would strengthen domestic capabilities and enable Indian technologies to find markets internationally, he said.
